ABSTRACT
The Handwritten Code Evaluator revolutionizes the assessment of handwritten programming
assignments by leveraging Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Machine Learning (ML).
Traditional manual evaluation is labor-intensive and error-prone; our system automates this
process with the following advancements:
● Digitization: Converts handwritten code into editable digital text using advanced OCR
techniques (e.g., Tesseract, Google Vision API).
● Code Evaluation: Compiles and executes the digitized code, checking for syntax errors,
logical correctness, and efficiency.
● Feedback Generation

Vision API).
● Code Evaluation: Compiles and executes the digitized code, checking for syntax errors,
logical correctness, and efficiency.
● Feedback Generation: Utilizes Natural Language Processing (NLP) to provide detailed,
actionable feedback to students, mimicking human grading.
● Scalability: Designed to handle bulk submissions, reducing grading time for educators
by over 70%.
This project bridges the gap between traditional handwritten submissions and modern automated
evaluation, ensuring accuracy, fairness, and efficiency in academic assessments.

2.2 SUMMARY
Our Handwritten Code Evaluator builds on key OCR advancements. Microsoft TrOCR (2021),
a transformer-based model, offers high handwriting recognition accuracy

Our Handwritten Code Evaluator builds on key OCR advancements. Microsoft TrOCR (2021),
a transformer-based model, offers high handwriting recognition accuracy and forms the core of
our system, despite its computational demands. Tesseract OCR (HP), an open-source
LSTM-based tool, serves as a customizable baseline but struggles with handwriting. The ACM
2020 paper on handwritten code recognition, using a CNN-RNN hybrid, effectively handles code
structure and inspired our post-processing and syntax correction modules. These works
collectively shaped our model’s architecture and strategy.

4.3 SUMMARY
The Handwritten Code Evaluator project aimed to recognize and evaluate handwritten Python
code using a deep learning-based system. The experimental setup consisted of three main
components: a diverse handwritten dataset, a CNN-LSTM model trained with CTC loss for text
recognition, and a secure backend for code evaluation.
Handwritten code samples were preprocessed (grayscale, normalization, augmentation) and used
to train a model capable of converting handwritten

for code evaluation.
Handwritten code samples were preprocessed (grayscale, normalization, augmentation) and used
to train a model capable of converting handwritten text to digital code. The recognized code was
then parsed and executed in a secure Python environment, with outputs or errors returned to the
user through a simple frontend interface.
Key Findings:
Challenges: Errors mainly came from unclear handwriting, special character misinterpretation,
and indentation issues.
Latency: Average processing time was 2–3 seconds per input.

CHAPTER 5 - CONCLUSION
5.1 CONCLUSION
The Handwritten Code Evaluator project has successfully developed a system capable of
recognizing handwritten code and evaluating it in real time. By utilizing deep learning

Handwritten Code Evaluator project has successfully developed a system capable of
recognizing handwritten code and evaluating it in real time. By utilizing deep learning
techniques, the project has achieved accurate recognition of diverse handwriting styles,
particularly in Python code. The backend system processes and evaluates the code efficiently,
while the frontend interface ensures an intuitive user experience.
The project has made significant progress in expanding the dataset, incorporating a variety of
Python code snippets and handwritten samples to improve the model's accuracy. This system
holds potential for real-world applications, including educational tools, assistance for individuals
with disabilities, and automating code review processes.

Abstract
Early and accurate detection of thoracic diseases remains a significant clinical challenge, particularly in
resource-constrained settings where radiologist expertise is limited. This paper presents a systematic
empirical evaluation of four distinct deep learning architectures for automated multi-class classification of
chest radiographs: a pure convolutional neural network baseline (ResNet50), a novel recurrent neural
network approach treating flattened radiographs as temporal sequences, and two hybrid variants combining
convolutional and Transformer-based mechanisms at different architectural levels. Our experiments
leverage a combined

convolutional and Transformer-based mechanisms at different architectural levels. Our experiments
leverage a combined dataset of 2,768 chest X-ray images spanning three disease classes—COVID-19,
pneumonia, and normal radiographs—sourced from publicly available medical imaging repositories. The
pure CNN baseline achieves 96.6% test accuracy with robust per-class performance. In contrast, the RNN
approach yields 91.7% accuracy, revealing that sequential modeling alone is insufficient for spatial medical
imaging tasks. Both hybrid architectures substantially improve upon these baselines: the true
CNN-Transformer hybrid reaches 97.5% macro-averaged F1 score,

hybrid architectures substantially improve upon these baselines: the true
CNN-Transformer hybrid reaches 97.5% macro-averaged F1 score, while the system-level ensemble of
ResNet50 and DenseNet121 achieves the highest performance at 97.7% accuracy with consistent class-wise
sensitivity. Our findings indicate that architectural diversity and attention-based feature refinement together
confer meaningful performance gains in thoracic disease detection. This work contributes novel insights
into the comparative efficacy of hybrid deep learning models in medical image analysis and offers practical
guidance for deploying automated screening systems in clinical settings.

1. Introduction
Thoracic diseases, including COVID-19, pneumonia, and tuberculosis, remain leading causes of morbidity
and mortality worldwide[1][2]. Chest X-ray radiography is the most widely deployed diagnostic imaging
modality for detecting such conditions due to its accessibility, low cost, and non-invasive nature[3].
However, the interpretation of radiographs is highly subjective and requires substantial expertise; diagnostic
errors are common, particularly in high-volume clinical settings or regions with radiologist shortages[4].
Consequently, computer-aided diagnostic

; diagnostic
errors are common, particularly in high-volume clinical settings or regions with radiologist shortages[4].
Consequently, computer-aided diagnostic (CAD) systems that augment radiologist decision-making have
become an active research area with significant clinical potential[5].
Deep learning has emerged as the dominant approach for automated medical image analysis over the past
decade[6][7]. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in image
classification tasks, including medical imaging, by learning hierarchical spatial features directly from pixel
data[8]. However, CNNs are inherently spatial in their operation and may struggle to model long-range
dependencies or temporal patterns that could be clinically relevant[9]. Recurrent neural networks (

inherently spatial in their operation and may struggle to model long-range
dependencies or temporal patterns that could be clinically relevant[9]. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs)
and their variants, such as long short-term memory (LSTM) cells and gated recurrent units (GRUs), excel at
capturing sequential dependencies and have shown promise in medical time-series analysis[10]. More
recently, Transformer architectures equipped with self-attention mechanisms have demonstrated superior
performance in numerous computer vision tasks by enabling direct modeling of global relationships
between image regions[11][12].
Despite the proliferation of individual architectures, few systematic studies directly compare these
paradigms on the same medical imaging dataset using equivalent preprocessing, data augmentation, and
evaluation protocols

architectures, few systematic studies directly compare these
paradigms on the same medical imaging dataset using equivalent preprocessing, data augmentation, and
evaluation protocols. Furthermore, hybrid approaches that combine complementary architectural strengths
remain underexplored in the thoracic disease detection domain[13]. This work addresses these gaps by
conducting a rigorous comparative evaluation of pure CNN, pure RNN, and two hybrid variants on a
standardized multi-class chest X-ray classification task. Our primary objectives are:
(i) To benchmark a ResNet50 baseline CNN and establish its performance as a reference standard;
(ii) To evaluate a novel RNN approach in which radiographs are reinterpreted as spatial sequences, testing
whether temporal modeling adds value beyond convolutional feature extraction;

whether temporal modeling adds value beyond convolutional feature extraction;
(iii) To develop and assess two hybrid architectures—a true CNN-Transformer fusion and a system-level
ensemble—to determine whether combining architectural paradigms yields synergistic performance
improvements;
(iv) To provide transparent, reproducible results suitable for comparison with future studies and potential
clinical deployment.
2. Related Work
2.1
CNN-based approaches to chest X-ray classification
The application of deep convolutional neural networks to medical image analysis has been extensively
studied[14][15]. Rajpurkar et al.[16] pioneered the use of deep CNNs for chest X-ray

has been extensively
studied[14][15]. Rajpurkar et al.[16] pioneered the use of deep CNNs for chest X-ray classification with
their CheXNet model, a 121-layer DenseNet pretrained on ImageNet, which achieved radiologist-level
performance on a large-scale dataset. Subsequent work has leveraged transfer learning, fine-tuning
pretrained backbones such as ResNet, EfficientNet, and Vision Transformers on domain-specific thoracic
datasets[17][18]. The general consensus in the literature is that CNNs with sufficient model capacity and
appropriate regularization converge rapidly and achieve high accuracy on chest X-ray tasks, often exceeding
95%[19][20].

2.2
Attention and Transformer mechanisms in medical imaging
The introduction of self-attention and Transformer architectures has catalyzed renewed interest in medical
image analysis[21]. Dosovitskiy et al.[22] proposed Vision Transformers (ViTs), which partition images into
patches and apply pure Transformer encoders, achieving competitive results on ImageNet and medical
imaging benchmarks. Hybrid approaches that interleave convolutional and Transformer blocks have proven

2.3
RNN and sequence-based approaches in medical imaging
While RNNs have dominated sequential data analysis in natural language processing and time-series
forecasting, their application to static medical images remains limited[27]. A few studies have attempted to
cast image classification as a sequential task—for instance, by processing image patches in raster order or
treating pixel rows as temporal sequences[28]. However, the reported benefits are marginal

task—for instance, by processing image patches in raster order or
treating pixel rows as temporal sequences[28]. However, the reported benefits are marginal, and RNNs are
generally considered ill-suited for spatial image data without significant adaptation[29]. Our work revisits
this question empirically on chest radiographs.
2.4
Ensemble and hybrid methods
Ensemble methods, which aggregate predictions from multiple models, have long been recognized as a
reliable path to performance improvements in machine learning[30][31]. In medical imaging, ensembles of
CNNs have been shown to reduce variance and improve robustness, particularly when the constituent
models are trained on different initializations or architectural variants[32]. Hybrid architectures

been shown to reduce variance and improve robustness, particularly when the constituent
models are trained on different initializations or architectural variants[32]. Hybrid architectures that
combine CNN and attention mechanisms within a single end-to-end model have also shown promise,
though systematic comparisons on medical datasets remain sparse[33][34].

5. Discussion
5.1
Interpretation of architecture-specific findings
The comparative results offer several insights into the relative merits of distinct deep learning paradigms for
thoracic disease detection:
CNN baseline performance: The ResNet50 baseline achieved 96.6% accuracy with balanced per-class
performance, confirming the well-established suitability of CNNs for spatial image analysis

ResNet50 baseline achieved 96.6% accuracy with balanced per-class
performance, confirming the well-established suitability of CNNs for spatial image analysis. The rapid
convergence and low validation loss indicate that convolutional feature hierarchies—local edges at early
layers, progressively abstract textures and shapes at deeper layers—align well with the diagnostic patterns
visible in chest radiographs. This finding is consistent with extensive prior literature and validates ResNet50
as a reliable reference standard[38][39].
RNN limitations: The pure RNN approach, while novel in its application to static radiographs,
underperformed both CNN-based methods. The 91.7% accuracy and particularly poor Normal-class
detection (88.8%

underperformed both CNN-based methods. The 91.7% accuracy and particularly poor Normal-class
detection (88.8% recall) suggest that interpreting a 224 × 224 radiograph as a sequence of 224 pixel-rows is
poorly matched to the spatial structure of diagnostic patterns. Thoracic diseases present localized opacities
or patterns (e.g., infiltrates in pneumonia, diffuse consolidation in COVID-19) that are not inherently
sequential along pixel rows. The RNN's strength in capturing long-range temporal dependencies offers no
advantage when applied to static 2D images. This outcome aligns with the broader finding that RNNs are
fundamentally unsuited for spatial

applied to static 2D images. This outcome aligns with the broader finding that RNNs are
fundamentally unsuited for spatial data without substantial architectural modification[40].
Hybrid architectures—complementary gains: Both hybrid approaches marginally outperformed or
matched the CNN baseline:
● The CNN-Transformer hybrid (97.5% accuracy, 0.9733 macro F1) suggests that Transformer
self-attention can refine ResNet50 features by modeling global spatial relationships that
convolutional receptive fields might miss. However, the improvement is modest (~1% absolute
accuracy gain), implying that ResNet50 already captures most diagnostically relevant information.
● The system-level ensemble (97.7% accuracy

● The system-level ensemble (97.7% accuracy, 0.9800 macro F1) demonstrated that combining
ResNet50 and DenseNet121 predictions yields consistent gains across all metrics. This
improvement arises from architectural diversity: ResNet's skip connections and DenseNet's dense
connections learn different feature representations. When both models correctly classify a sample,
the ensemble reinforces this decision; when one errs, the other often recovers, resulting in net error
reduction. The 97.7% accuracy represents approximately a 1.1% absolute improvement over the

5.2
Clinical implications and deployment considerations
From a clinical perspective, all four models exceed reasonable performance thresholds for use as a
screening or triage tool. A 97.7% accuracy translates to a false positive rate of approximately 2.3%,
acceptable for preliminary radiological screening in many settings. However, the RNN's weaker
Normal-class performance (88.8% recall) would result in ~11% of healthy radiographs being flagged as
abnormal, potentially increasing radiologist workload with false alarms.

abnormal, potentially increasing radiologist workload with false alarms.
The superior ensemble and hybrid performance, by contrast, minimizes false negatives (particularly for
COVID-19 detection), which is clinically critical: missing a positive case poses greater harm than a false
alarm[42]. The marginal accuracy improvement from the ensemble (0.3% above the hybrid) may seem
minor numerically but could translate to ~4 additional correctly classified cases per 1,000 radiographs
screened in a real-world deployment.

5.3
Computational efficiency trade-offs
Model inference latency and computational cost should inform deployment decisions. ResNet50 is
substantially lighter than DenseNet121 and hybrid variants, with inference times around 10–15 ms per
image on standard GPU hardware. The ensemble requires two forward passes, doubling inference time,
while the CNN-Transformer hybrid incurs additional Transformer overhead (~5–10 ms) despite similar
parameter counts. In high-throughput settings (e.g., a radiology department processing hundreds of images
daily), the CNN baseline may be preferred given its speed and reasonable accuracy. Conversely, in
lower-volume or research contexts where maximizing accuracy is paramount, the ensemble justifies the
computational cost.

5.4
Limitations and future work
Several limitations warrant acknowledgment:
1. Dataset scope: Our evaluation uses 2,768 images across three classes. While sufficient for pilot
studies, larger multicenter datasets would strengthen generalization claims. Additionally, our
dataset comprises primarily frontal chest radiographs; lateral and oblique views, common in
clinical practice, were not included.
2. No statistical significance testing: We report raw metrics without confidence intervals or
hypothesis tests. Given the fixed test set size, the observed 1% difference between models may
reflect sampling variance rather than true

or
hypothesis tests. Given the fixed test set size, the observed 1% difference between models may
reflect sampling variance rather than true architecture superiority.
3. Limited hyperparameter exploration: Early stopping patience, learning rates, and regularization
strengths were held constant across models. Architecture-specific tuning might yield different
conclusions.
4. Absence of radiologist comparison: While our models exceed 96% accuracy, direct comparison
with radiologist performance on the same test set would contextualize clinical utility[43].
5. Reproducibility details: Although we provide hyperparameters, variations in random seeds,
CUDA versions, and hardware can subtly affect training dynamics. Full code release (e.g., via
GitHub) would facilitate reproduction

Future work should:
● Evaluate ensemble methods with learned weighting rather than simple averaging[44].
● Investigate explainability techniques (e.g., Grad-CAM, attention visualizations) to build clinician

● Conduct prospective validation on an independent external dataset.
● Explore domain adaptation techniques to transfer models trained on public datasets to
institution-specific imaging protocols[46].
6. Conclusion
This work presents a systematic empirical comparison of four deep learning architectures for automated
thoracic disease detection in chest radiographs: a ResNet50 CNN baseline, a BiLSTM RNN approach

deep learning architectures for automated
thoracic disease detection in chest radiographs: a ResNet50 CNN baseline, a BiLSTM RNN approach, a
CNN-Transformer hybrid, and a ResNet50 + DenseNet121 ensemble. Our key findings are:
1. Pure CNNs remain highly effective: The ResNet50 baseline achieved 96.6% test accuracy with
robust per-class performance, validating the continued suitability of convolution-based
architectures for medical image classification.
2. Recurrent models are ill-suited for static radiographs: The pure RNN attained only 91.7%
accuracy, with particularly weak Normal-class detection, confirming that sequential modeling
provides no advantage for spatial image data without fundamental architectural

91.7%
accuracy, with particularly weak Normal-class detection, confirming that sequential modeling
provides no advantage for spatial image data without fundamental architectural innovations.
3. Hybrid approaches confer modest but meaningful gains: The CNN-Transformer hybrid and the
ResNet50 + DenseNet121 ensemble both achieved ~97.5–97.7% accuracy, outperforming the
baseline by approximately 1%. These results indicate that architectural complementarity—whether
through attention refinement or ensemble diversity—offers a practical path to improved
performance.
4. Ensemble methods maximize accuracy within practical constraints: The system-level
ensemble achieved the highest macro F1 score (0.98) and best per-class sensitivity, making it a
robust choice for clinical

-level
ensemble achieved the highest macro F1 score (0.98) and best per-class sensitivity, making it a
robust choice for clinical deployment when computational resources permit.
Our systematic evaluation fills a gap in the thoracic disease detection literature by directly comparing
multiple paradigms under controlled conditions. The findings support the use of either the
CNN-Transformer hybrid or ensemble approaches for real-world applications seeking to maximize
diagnostic accuracy. More broadly, this work demonstrates the value of empirical comparison across
architectural families and provides a template for similar studies in medical imaging.
